passage:
In the small town of Hosapete, Kiran had saved from his tuition job for a new phone. For three weeks he compared models every night: thirty-one tabs, battery charts, camera tests.
At the mobile shop near the bus stand, Salma, the shopkeeper, laid out five boxes. He held each one, checked his notes, and asked about another model that wasn't in stock. At last he chose the blue one.
Walking home past the temple, he was already watching a review of a different phone, frowning.
"Happy?" asked his cousin at dinner.
"It's fine," Kiran said, and scrolled through the other phone's photos again.

qa.q: How many tabs did Kiran have open while comparing phones?
qa.a: Thirty-one tabs, with battery charts and camera tests.

qa.q: Why does Kiran feel only 'fine' about the phone he chose?
qa.a: After comparing so many models, he keeps imagining the other phones might have been better, so the blue one feels less satisfying.

qa.q: What could Kiran do next time before comparing phones?
qa.a: He could list the three things he most needs and look only at phones that meet them, so there are fewer options to second-guess.

qa.q: How might Salma feel after Kiran asks about a phone that isn't in stock?
qa.a: Salma might feel a little tired or worried about losing the sale, having already laid out five boxes for him.

grounding: Shows a young man who compares many phones, stays unsure, and is less pleased with his final choice.

passage:
In a café in Madrid, Alejandro had a spreadsheet of twenty-four master's programmes: Lisbon, Utrecht, Lyon, Milan. Columns for fees, rankings, weather, even distance to the sea. His friend Freya watched him add another row.
"You said you'd decide in March," Freya said. "It's May."
"I just want to be sure."
In June he finally picked Utrecht and sent the form. That evening, instead of celebrating, he scrolled through the Lyon course page again. "Lyon had that river," he murmured.
Freya put down the cup. "Last time you had three options and chose your bachelor's in ten minutes. You loved it."
Alejandro shrugged and kept scrolling.

qa.q: Which programme did Alejandro finally pick?
qa.a: In June he finally picked Utrecht and sent the form.

qa.q: What does Alejandro's scrolling on the Lyon page suggest he feels after choosing?
qa.a: It suggests he still feels unsure and slightly regretful, as if one of the other twenty-three options might have been the right one.

qa.q: What could Alejandro learn from how he chose his bachelor's?
qa.a: He could narrow to a few options that meet his key needs and decide quickly, as he did with three options before and ended up loving it.

qa.q: How does Freya see Alejandro's months of comparing?
qa.a: Freya sees him stuck and unhappy, and remembers that fewer choices once made him quick and content.

grounding: Shows a student abroad who compares dozens of programmes, delays, and feels less satisfied once he chooses.

passage:
At the college academic office, next semester's elective list ran to forty-two courses. Sameer had printed it, highlighted it in four colours, and asked Minakshi, the counsellor, three times about credit rules. His classmate Bhavna had picked her two in a day, from the five her department suggested.
On the last day of registration, Sameer was still at the office window, switching between photography, urban design and game theory. He clicked urban design at 4:55 p.m.
The next week, while Bhavna talked excitedly about her pottery class, Sameer sat through his first lecture reading the photography course outline on his phone.

qa.q: How many courses were on the elective list?
qa.a: The elective list ran to forty-two courses.

qa.q: Why might Sameer keep reading the photography outline during his lecture?
qa.a: With so many options weighed, he feels uncertain he chose right, so the course he didn't pick keeps pulling at him.

qa.q: What would you advise Sameer to try next semester?
qa.a: Start from a short list, like the five Bhavna's department suggested, and pick early instead of weighing all forty-two.

qa.q: How does Bhavna's experience differ from Sameer's?
qa.a: Bhavna chose from five in a day and is excited about pottery, while Sameer chose from forty-two at the last minute and feels unsettled.

grounding: Shows a student who weighs a huge elective list, decides late, and feels less content than a classmate who had fewer options.

passage:
Dear Chandrika Didi,
You asked how counselling went. I've filled my choices, finally. Here's the embarrassing part. The portal allowed a hundred options, so I researched a hundred and twelve colleges. Placements, hostel photos, alumni posts, even canteen reviews. Every night I reordered the list. Ma said, "You look like you haven't slept in a month," and she was right.
I got my fourth choice, a decent college in Nagpur with the branch I wanted. And still I keep opening the list, thinking number nine had a better lab, number twenty-three a nicer campus. When you chose your college you only had three to look at, and you seem so happy there.
Is that strange? I got what I wanted and I feel like I lost something.
Your cousin brother,
Amandeep

qa.q: How many colleges did Amandeep research?
qa.a: He researched a hundred and twelve colleges.

qa.q: Why does Amandeep feel he lost something even after getting his fourth choice?
qa.a: Having studied so many colleges, he can picture what each one had that his lacks, so he isn't sure he got the best and feels less content.

qa.q: What choice could Amandeep make now that the seat is his?
qa.a: He could close the list for good and look at what the Nagpur college gives him, like the branch he wanted, instead of comparing it with options he no longer has.

qa.q: How might Chandrika see her own college choice after reading this letter?
qa.a: She might realise that having only three to look at helped her feel settled, and feel sorry that the long list has cost her cousin his peace.

grounding: A student compares over a hundred colleges, stays unsure and feels less satisfied with the seat he gets than a cousin who had only three options.

passage: Damini, you asked why I still haven't started learning Japanese. Okay, the truth. I downloaded fourteen language apps. Fourteen. I made a table: which has audio, which has writing drills, which has streaks, which has a live tutor. I read reviews till two in the morning, and every review said a different app was best. After three weeks I picked one. And honestly? Every time a lesson feels slow, I think, the green one would've been better, or the one with video. My mother laughed and said, "Tanvir, my son, the app inspector." I haven't opened any of them in five days. When my dad learned German years ago, he had one book. One. And he finished it.

qa.q: How many language apps did Tanvir download?
qa.a: He downloaded fourteen language apps.

qa.q: Why does a slow lesson make Tanvir think another app would have been better?
qa.a: Tanvir feels doubtful and a bit regretful, because after comparing fourteen apps he knows every other app's strong points, so the one he chose never feels good enough.

qa.q: What could Tanvir choose to do now so he actually starts?
qa.a: He could delete every app but the one he picked and stick with it for a month, treating it like his dad's single book instead of comparing again.

qa.q: What might Damini think on hearing that Tanvir hasn't opened any app in five days?
qa.a: Damini might find it funny but also feel a bit sorry for Tanvir, seeing that all the comparing has drained his excitement about Japanese 😅

grounding: A young man compares fourteen apps, finally picks one and feels less satisfied with it than his father was with a single book.

passage: Pankaj, you've had forty college tabs open for a month, haven't you? Your Santosh chacha did the same, just with paper. At nineteen, I had the fat admissions guide, every college in Maharashtra, and I read it like a novel. I made lists, then lists of lists: fees, hostels, placements, the canteen, the colour of the buildings in the photos. I changed my mind every week. Finally the deadline came and I picked the one in Sangli. And for the whole first year, I kept thinking about the others. Maybe Pune had better labs. Maybe Kolhapur had nicer friends. Your chachi, who had looked at just three colleges, loved hers. It took me a year to see that Sangli was good. What stole my happiness wasn't the college. It was the thirty I didn't choose.

qa.q: Which college did young Santosh finally pick?
qa.a: He picked the one in Sangli.

qa.q: Why did young Santosh keep thinking about other colleges during his first year?
qa.a: He felt restless and unsatisfied, because after comparing so many, every college he hadn't chosen seemed like it might have been better.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Chacha's story?
qa.a: Seeing, a year later, that Sangli was good and that his unhappiness came from the thirty colleges he didn't choose.

qa.q: How did Chachi's college choice feel different for her?
qa.a: Chachi looked at just three colleges and loved the one she picked, with far less to regret.

grounding: Shows a student comparing dozens of colleges, staying unsure, and feeling less satisfied with the final pick.

passage: Zubin's old phone died two days before his internship started, he had exactly one month's stipend to spend, and the online sale ended at midnight. So he did what he always did: he compared. Thirty-one tabs. Camera scores, battery tests, video reviews, forum arguments. Rajni, sitting on his bed, watched him switch between the same three phones for an hour. "They're all fine, Zubin." "But one of them is the best." At 11:52 he panicked and bought the blue one. It arrived on Tuesday, worked perfectly, and he hated it. Every time he opened it he thought of the grey one's better camera and the black one's longer battery. "If you'd only looked at three," Rajni said, "you'd love this one." He knew she was right, which made it worse.

qa.q: How many tabs did Zubin have open?
qa.a: Zubin had thirty-one tabs open.

qa.q: Why does Zubin hate a phone that works perfectly?
qa.a: Zubin feels dissatisfied and regretful, because after comparing so many, he keeps thinking about the features of the phones he didn't buy.

qa.q: What could Zubin do the next time he has to buy something like this?
qa.a: Set two or three must-haves first, shortlist three options, and pick a good-enough one without reopening the others.

qa.q: How does Rajni see the whole search?
qa.a: Rajni sees that all the phones were fine, and that the endless comparing, not the phone, is making Zubin unhappy.

grounding: Shows a student comparing dozens of phones under time pressure, then feeling unhappy with a perfectly good choice.

passage: In their hostel room in Hyderabad, Siddharth had tried fourteen planner apps in three weeks. Each promised to finally organise his life. He would download one, spend an evening setting up colours and tags, read that another was better, delete it, and start again. His actual assignments sat untouched. "Which one are you on now?" Samir asked from the other bed, writing in a cheap spiral notebook. "The one with the tree that grows. But the one with the calendar view might be better." "You said that about the tree." Siddharth sighed. None of them felt right, because there was always another. Samir held up the notebook. "One. Never looked at another." Siddharth laughed, then stopped. He deleted all the apps but one, and opened his first assignment.

qa.q: What does Samir write in?
qa.a: Samir writes in a cheap spiral notebook.

qa.q: Why does no planner app feel right to Siddharth?
qa.a: Siddharth feels restless and unsatisfied, because with so many options there is always another app that might be better.

qa.q: What did Siddharth finally do, and why was it a good move?
qa.a: He deleted all but one app and opened his first assignment, ending the search so the actual work could start.

qa.q: How does Samir see Siddharth's search?
qa.a: Samir sees it as time lost choosing tools, and shows that one plain notebook, never compared, works fine.

grounding: Shows a student trying app after app, never satisfied because another might be better, until choosing to stop.

passage:
"Yogesh, it's been three weeks. Just buy a phone."

"Simran, I have a spreadsheet with twenty-six models."

"Twenty-six?"

"Camera scores, battery, weight, two colours each. Every time I pick one, another review says the other is better."

"Your old phone died on Monday. You're using my charger."

"Fine. Fine. I'm ordering the grey one."

A week later Simran found him scrolling reviews again.

"You got it already!"

"I know. But the other one has a better night camera. Maybe I should return it."

"Is anything wrong with yours?"

"No," Yogesh admitted. "It's good. It just doesn't feel good."

qa.q: How many phone models were on Yogesh's spreadsheet?
qa.a: His spreadsheet had twenty-six models.

qa.q: Why does Yogesh say the phone "just doesn't feel good" even though nothing is wrong with it?
qa.a: After comparing so many options he feels dissatisfied and unsure, because every model he skipped seems like it might have been better.

qa.q: What could Yogesh try next time he has to choose a phone?
qa.a: He could pick three things that matter most, shortlist two or three phones, choose one and stop reading reviews after buying.

qa.q: How might Simran see Yogesh's endless searching?
qa.a: Simran seems amused but also tired of it, especially since he is still using her charger.

grounding: A student compares dozens of phones, stays unsure and feels less satisfied with his final choice.

passage:
Last spring I had to choose a master's programme. I thought more options meant a better choice, so I kept adding colleges. At one point there were forty tabs open on my laptop. My roommate Divyansh chose his course in a week from a list of four. I kept going for two months, comparing fees, rankings, hostel photos, alumni posts.

I finally picked a good course in Hyderabad. It's genuinely fine. The faculty are kind, the library is open late. But almost every week I still wonder about the one in Bengaluru or the one abroad I never applied to.

Divyansh, with his list of four, seems perfectly happy. I'm Vijay, and I'm starting to think my forty tabs cost me more than time.

qa.q: How many tabs were open on Vijay's laptop at one point?
qa.a: At one point there were forty tabs open on the laptop.

qa.q: What does Vijay feel about the course he chose, and why?
qa.a: Vijay feels restless and dissatisfied despite the course being fine, because comparing so many options leaves the others still pulling at attention.

qa.q: What would you advise Vijay the next time a big choice comes up?
qa.a: Decide on a few must-have criteria first and limit the list to a handful, as Divyansh did, then stop comparing once the choice is made.

qa.q: How might Divyansh experience his own choice differently from Vijay?
qa.a: Divyansh seems content and settled because he compared only four courses and has fewer what-ifs to carry.

grounding: A student compares dozens of colleges, stays unsure, and feels less satisfied with the final choice than a peer with fewer options.

passage:
Note by the college placement counsellor, Wednesday.

Francis came in again today to talk about internships. He had applied to four but had shortlisted thirty-one, and he showed me his notes on each. He said he had turned down an offer from a design studio last week because a friend, Vijay, mentioned a bigger firm might open applications soon. That firm has not opened anything.

Francis kept saying, "What if I pick wrong?" He rubbed his forehead and looked tired.

I asked him to write the three things he most wants from an internship and cross out any option missing two of them. The list dropped to five. He will choose one by Friday, and we will meet then.

qa.q: How many internships had Francis shortlisted?
qa.a: Francis had shortlisted thirty-one internships.

qa.q: What does Francis's repeated question "What if I pick wrong?" suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he feels anxious and stuck, since each extra option makes every choice seem less certain.

qa.q: Why was the counsellor's three-criteria exercise a useful step?
qa.a: It cut thirty-one options to five, making a decision by Friday possible and less draining.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel if he learned his comment led Francis to turn down the studio?
qa.a: Vijay might feel uncomfortable or a little guilty, since a passing remark cost his friend a real offer.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a student comparing dozens of options, staying unsure and losing a good choice while searching.

Sunday, 1 a.m.
Finally bought the laptop. After three weeks. I compared thirty-four models on a spreadsheet: processor, weight, battery, screen, reviews, price. Every time I thought I'd decided, another video said something else was better.
Binita bought hers in one afternoon. Three options at the shop, chose the middle one, done. She loves it.
Mine arrived today. It's good. It's actually great. But I keep thinking about model 17, the lighter one. And model 22 had a better screen. I'm sitting here with a great laptop, feeling like I lost.
Note to self for next time: pick three things that matter, pick three models, stop.
Bhupen

qa.q: Why does Bhupen feel like losing despite having a great laptop?

passage:
The mobile shop on the main road of Hoshiarpur had forty phones in the glass case, and Divyansh had been inside for two hours. The shopkeeper had brought out eleven, one by one. Camera, battery, storage, colour.
"This one," Divyansh said finally. Then, "No, wait, show the blue one again."
Jasleen, waiting outside on her scooter, came in. "You said you only need a good battery and a camera for your project photos."
"Yes, but this one has more storage, and that one is thinner."
He bought the thinner one. On the way home, riding pillion, he kept looking at it. "I think the other camera was better," he said. "Should I go back?"
Jasleen sighed. "You chose from eleven. Any of them would have been fine. Let this one be good."

qa.q: How many phones did the shopkeeper bring out?
qa.a: The shopkeeper brought out eleven phones.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh want to go back after buying?
qa.a: Divyansh felt unsure and dissatisfied, because with eleven options he kept wondering whether another camera was better.

qa.q: What could Divyansh do to feel happier with a choice like this?
qa.a: Divyansh could stick to the two things that mattered, battery and camera, compare a few phones and then let the choice be good.

qa.q: How does Jasleen feel after two hours?
qa.a: Jasleen is patient but tired and a bit exasperated, trying to help Divyansh accept a good choice.

grounding: Shows a student who compares many phones, stays unsure and feels less satisfied with the final choice.

passage:
By the end of the January sales in Manchester, Sami's spreadsheet held twenty-three phones, with columns for battery, camera, weight and reviews. He had watched so many comparison videos that the phones blurred into one glossy rectangle.
"Just pick," Amara said, scrolling on the one she had bought in ten minutes at the corner shop. "Mine's great."
On the last day of the sale, after the top two sold out, he finally clicked "buy" on the one ranked third.
It arrived on Thursday. It was fast and the photos were sharp. But that night Sami opened the spreadsheet again and stared at numbers one and two. "Maybe the second one's battery..." he muttered.
Amara, eating toast across the table, shook her head. "You've got a good phone and you're still sulking about two you don't own."

qa.q: How many phones were in Sami's spreadsheet?
qa.a: Twenty-three phones.

qa.q: Why is Sami still unsatisfied with a phone that works well?
qa.a: Having compared so many, he feels unsure and a bit regretful, since each phone he didn't buy still seems like it might have been better.

qa.q: What could Sami try the next time he has to choose?
qa.a: He could decide the three features that matter most, cut the list to a shortlist of three, and stop comparing once he has bought.

qa.q: How does Amara see Sami's spreadsheet habit?
qa.a: She finds it puzzling, because she chose hers in ten minutes and is happy with it, while he sulks about phones he doesn't own.

grounding: Shows a student comparing dozens of phones and feeling less satisfied with the final pick than a simpler choice would allow.
